newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's Petrozuata to produce 30kbpd by 1998.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's Petrozuata to produce 30kbpd by 1998.

text.p: Venezuela's extra-heavy Orinoco oil venture with U.S. Conoco is planning to drill its first well in August this year and should be pumping 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) 12 months later, the project leader said on Wednesday.

Warren Hairford, general manager of the $2.2 billion Petrozuata joint venture, said the partners would have spent $630 million and committed $1 billion to the project by the end of 1997. Venezuelan state oil subsidiary Maraven is a 50 percent partner in the scheme.
The project envisages 120,000 bpd extra-heavy oil production in the Orinoco, two pipelines to the Caribbean port of Jose and a billion-dollar conversion plant in Jose to lighten the crude.

Financing is expected to be finalised by next month when a tender to build the Jose plant is due to be announced. Banking sources in New York say the senior debt has received an investment grade by Moody Investor Service.

Hairford said the pipeline would be completed in May/June 1998, just before production comes on line. Between 65 and 100 wells would be drilled and output would rise from 30,000 bpd to peak at 120,000 bpd in 2000 when the conversion plant is scheduled to start running.
A team in Maraven was studying how to sell the extra-heavy (9 API) crude during the intervening two years and Hairford expected a decision in mid-July.
When the conversion plant is running, Hairford said two- thirds of the synthetic crude (70,000 bpd) would go to Conoco's 226,000 bpd Lake Charles refinery in Louisiana, U.S.A.
This supply deal did not involve Venezuela's state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela taking a stake in the refinery, Conoco chief executive Archie Dunham said.
One third (35,000 bpd) of the synthetic crude would go to Maraven's 305,000 bpd Cardon refinery on Venezuela's north coast.
Lake Charles would take a heavier 20-21 API grade, while Cardon would take a 25-26 API oil, Hairford added.

In addition to 104,000 bpd of synthetic crude, the Jose plant will produce about 3,500 bpd of liqufied petroleum gas (LPG) to be marketed by Venezuela's Corpoven and some gas oil which Petrozuata would sell on the open market.
